title: 'Unjustifiable and unacceptable': Family calls for inquiry into man's death during Montreal police intervention
article: Marcelina Isidro broke down in tears on Wednesday as she tried to explain how difficult the last few weeks have been since her son, Abisay Cruz, died after a Montreal police intervention at her St-Michel apartment.
When it became clear she couldn't speak through her grief, Cruz's younger brother, Josué, stepped in to read a prepared statement on behalf of the family.
"When my brother Abisay died in the hands of the police, he was in a state of crisis. He needed help," said Josué, 23. "His death is completely unjustifiable and unacceptable."
The family called a news conference as it pushes for answers about how Cruz died and the way police treated the 29-year-old father during the intervention.
Authorities have released few details about what happened the morning in question.

According to the Bureau des enquêtes indépendantes (BEI), which investigates whenever a person dies or is seriously injured during a police intervention in Quebec, officers were called to the apartment around 8 a.m. on March 30 to respond to a person in crisis.
A physical altercation ensued between Cruz and the officers, the BEI said, and he lost consciousness after being subdued. He was taken to a hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.

Parts of the intervention were caught on video and witnessed by neighbours. The Center for Research-Action on Race Relations, which is assisting the family, argues the evidence points to police using excessive force.

In one video posted to social media, officers can be seen on the second-floor apartment's balcony with Cruz. One is attempting to kick down the door, while another keeps Cruz on the floor, pressing his knee into his back. Cruz can be heard groaning and writhing in pain.

Police eventually carried Cruz into the apartment, the family says. In a video they shared on Wednesday, what appears to be blood splatter can be seen on the floor, in addition to smashed household items. Another video shows a paramedic aggressively attempting resuscitation techniques on Cruz in the ambulance.
The family is now asking for a public coroner's inquest to shed light on exactly what went wrong.
Their lawyer, René Saint-Léger, asked why police resorted to using force when responding to a man in crisis, describing it as the latest in a long list of similar cases.

Saint-Léger said Cruz's death brings to mind the cases of Alain Magloire, an unhoused man shot by Montreal police while in crisis in 2014, and George Floyd, a Black man who died while a police officer in Minneapolis pressed a knee to his neck in 2020.
Saint-Léger could not speak to why Cruz was in crisis or what led to police being called.
"But at the same time, if you get there and you see somebody in distress, what is the conduct you should have?" he asked. "What is the attitude to take? Why did it have to go to that extreme?"
CRARR executive director Fo Niemi said the case raises questions about whether police treated Cruz differently because of his Latin American background.
Niemi also questioned if systemic issues, such as the police force's relationship with the community in St-Michel, played a role in how police responded.

"The question is why such excessive force when the policy directive is (to use) de-escalation," Niemi said. "Especially when someone is in a visible state of distress and obviously in need of mental health support."
The Montreal police department did not respond to a request for comment by deadline.
Cruz's death had sparked rallies and protests after videos of the intervention spread online, including one march that ended with six arrests.
The family told reporters Wednesday they do not encourage people to protest and would rather those who wish to support them focus their energy toward demanding a public inquest.
Josué spoke fondly of his older brother, describing him as a good person who loved his nine-year-old son.
"He always wanted to make the people around him laugh," he said.
The family has not yet received an autopsy report regarding Cruz's death, he said, nor have they been visited by the BEI or Montreal police since that day, which has further fuelled their distrust.
He worries they will never find peace without answers.
"We want there to be justice, because no one deserves to be treated this way," Josué said. "And I just hope this doesn't happen to anyone else, because it's a very, very deep pain."
